articles.text: Egg Drop on final day the highlight Piedmont Cub Scouts enjoyed a wide range of arts and crafts, learned valuable Scout skills, and participated in STEM-related activities at the Piedmont Council’s annual Cub Scout Day Camp. A tradition for more than 55 years, the day camp welcomes first through fifth graders for five afternoons of activities in Dracena Park. The highlight each year is an egg drop facilitated by the Fire Department and its 75-foot extension ladder This year’s camp ran from Monday to Friday, June 10-14. “For a lot of our kids it’s a tradition; many attend for all five years,” said Eris Turner, Program Manager with the Piedmont Council. “We had several campers who were sad they had to leave early on certain days because of other commitments.” Nearly 20 Cub Scouts were repeat attendees. Each day the campers cycled through six stations – cooking, crafts, Den time, Scout skills, sports and STEM activities, each with unique daily activities inspired by this year’s camp theme, “Outdoor Adventure.” Some of these activities included making decorative sun catchers out of recycled water bottles, designing Den flags, creating cheers, learning how to do a flag ceremony, playing “Ranger Says” (an activity similar to “Simon Says”), making a homemade battery by using with dirt and making homemade ice cream. The Day Camp also presents leadership opportunities for older Scouts. The plague of catalytic converter thefts Editor The following letter was sent to Police Chief Jeremy Bowers. Dear Chief Bowers, I am writing this as an open letter to you because I believe many Piedmont residents have a similar concern. A few weeks ago, the catalytic converter on my Prius was stolen ... for the second time. The CAT was cut out despite my having installed a protective plate. “That happens a lot,” the responding police officer told me, “The thieves know how to cut around those protective plates, it just takes them a few minutes longer.” I don’t fault the Piedmont Police for not being able to catch the thieves in the act; they are in and out of Piedmont very quickly. But I do wonder what our police department is doing, and can do, to stem this rampant crime. Here are two suggestions. I’d like to know Piedmont’s reaction. 1) This is a regional problem. It must be solved with cooperative effort of all the police departments in Alameda County, the County sheriff, and probably all the counties in the Bay Area. CAT thieves should not be safe from apprehension simply by crossing jurisdictional lines. 2) A joint-agency force must investigate and apprehend the criminals at the top of the money chain. Low-level thieves cut out the CATs, and then take them to some kind of chop shop where the valuable platinum elements are removed. Then the platinum is sent to some kind of refinery where it is molded into a high-priced, saleable resource. The money for this enterprise flows down the chain: from the refiner to the chop shop to the street thief. This plague of thefts can only be stopped by identifying and apprehending the perpetrators at the top of the money chain. What is Piedmont doing, in collaboration with other law enforcement agencies, to stop these CAT thefts at the source of the problem? I have spent money on a new CAT and a new blocking plate, knowing that this just makes it slightly more difficult for the CAT thieves. What else can a Piedmont resident do besides call on our Police Chief to participate in, or establish if necessary, a region-wide effort to stop the CAT thieves’ money source? –Bruce Joffe Piedmont resident ROLAND LAZZAROTTO, Parade Starter I liked the time we had horses and a guy assigned to walk behind the horses to clean up after them. articles.text: Photo by Greg Slatoff The Piedmont Community Band marches in last year’s 4th of July Parade with its large banner. celebrate its 40th anniversary at this year’s 4th of July parade. The band is comprised of amateur and professional musicians – all volunteers – who can’t resist the challenge of playing music while marching in formation. Dressed in blue pants, white shirts and a red kerchief, they are led each year by Ken Kawaichi dressed as Emperor Norton, that time-honored resident of San Francisco who proclaimed himself “Emperor of the United States” in 1859, despite having no formal political power. Kawaichi has the distinction of being the only person to march the length of the parade route backwards. Piedmont Community Band was established in 1984 by then-student Jane Reed with the assistance of PHS Music Director Alan Harvey. “The first thing Mr. Harvey told me was ‘We have no marching equipment,’” she laughed. It was a beginning strongly reminiscent of the Meredith Willson musical, The Music Man, except the band to be created was to include adults and schoolkids. Undaunted, Reed knew she could count on the community for help. Daughters of the American Revolution donated $100 to help buy straps for the instruments and donations came in little by little, year after year. The Piedmont Recreation Department donated a banner in subsequent years. “It was a community effort,” Reed explained. The band’s “one rehearsal, one performance” mantra evolved out of necessity. “I was trying to get other high school kids, who are typically very busy, to set aside one evening to practice before we played in the parade. So, we just did one practice, hoping that enough students would come and that we would look okay on the parade day,” recalled Reed. The Community Band’s first performance was in the parade in 1984. “That first year was a little bit difficult because none of these kids had marched and played at the same time. So they were learning to do that,” she said. Greg Slatoff, a longtime member of the band, stepped forward this year as one of its directors, picking up the reins of Ray Per- 4th of July Parade man, who led the band until his death in 2017. Slatoff is best known for organizing the Piedmont Jazz Festival each year. He said he joined the band for the wonderful, near romantic feeling it gives him. “It just reminds you of everything right with America. It’s a time when you’re marching down Highland and you’re blowing your horn with your friends and neighbors around you,” he said. “I mean, that’s just as good as it gets.” The band is also known for its loose structure and hierarchy. Musicians who show up for the annual rehearsal are welcomed into the lineup with open arms. “It’s kind of ‘ragged, but right’ in that sense,” explained Slatoff. “We have some ringers. We’ve got people that are from the USC band who really know what they’re doing, And then they have bozos like me that sort of play the tenor saxophone and sort of fumble their way through it,” he joked. “We love doing it because we love seeing it,” added Reed, also a saxophone player. “We love seeing the band every year. I really feel it’s important to have music in the parade,” said Reed. Keeping with tradition, the band meets once a year on the evening of July 2 on Dracena Avenue for a one-block street. The band typically plays three standard pieces of music, anchored by the University of Wisconsin fight song, “On Wisconsin.” All musicians – adults and older students – with an interest in being part of the band aencouraged to contact Greg Slatoff at goslatoff@yahoo.com. New band members will be sent copies of all music to be played before the parade.

articles.text: Book is a celebration and description of what makes great cartoons great The book Funny Stuff: How Great Cartoonists Make Great Cartoons, co-authored by Piedmont cartoonist Phil Witte and former Piedmont resident Rex Hesner, will be released nationally in hard cover next month on July 16. The book is a 135-page exploration of comics and cartoons with a particular emphasis on the art form of the single-panel cartoon. The pages contain over 100 cartoons which the authors use to spark discussions about process, inspiration, art and diversity in the world of cartooning. articles.text: School districts in California must present a Local Control Accountability Plan (LCAP) every three years for their school board and county boards to approve. Assistant Superintendent Ariel Dolowich delivered a comprehensive initial public hearing during the June 12 school board meeting, and the LCAP for 2024-27 stands to be approved in tonight’s, June 26, meeting. “This was a heavy lift. There were so many different things about it and this was a three-year LCAP. We were aligning with the strategic plan,” said Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen of the 87-page report. Goal #1: Creating an Environment to Thrive Goal #2: Investing in Outstanding Academics Goal #3: Partnering Beyond the Classroom Goal #4: Building for Operational Excellence Next year, for the first time, Piedmont will offer Independent Study on a third-party platform, with Irma Munoz Daniels as liaison. Superintendent Jennifer Hawn added her excitement about Independent Study, which can be hybrid as well. “[Independent Study] is a program gap in our district, which could build our enrollment, and it could offer an alternative option for students who need it,” said Hawn. The broadest direction for the district is its Strategic Plan. The LCAP functions within the strategic plan. For individual concerns or needs the district looks specifically to the Single Plan for Student Achievement (SPSA). In tonight’s school board meeting the LCAP will receive further consideration and is subject to further public comment before board approval.
articles.title: LCAP delivers three-year vision for Piedmont schools

pages.text: 6 Wednesday, June 26, 2024 Summer Thoughts By Randall Grayson Are you the parent of a schoolaged child? This is for you. Why did you decide to have children? What brings you joy in parenting now? And most importantly, how can you make the most of this precious time? Is it their laughter, their curiosity, or watching them grow and learn? Perhaps it is the way they see the world with fresh eyes? These are the moments that make parenthood so rewarding. A look at the stats • 75% of the time we spend with our kids in our lifetime will be spent by age 12. • During an average school week, parents spend less than an hour a day truly engaged with their children—playing games, taking walks, or sharing distraction-free meals. • Parents spend about 20 more minutes a day with children in the summer than during the school year. • Pondering: how much time do you spend, and would you like to spend? • With 2 hours a day during the summer weekdays, and 6 hours each day over the weekend, a 10-week summer could offer an extra 220 hours of quality time – that’s equivalent to over 9 full days. “Quality time” isn’t just about being in the same room; it’s about full engagement – playing, talking, sharing meals without screens, or simply being present. It’s not about elaborate plans or expensive outings; it’s about connection. Below are some broad, varied ideas to get your juices flowing. Outdoor Activities • Outdoor Adventures: Hike, camp, or explore local parks. Nature provides endless opportunities for bonding and learning. • Gardening: Plant and tend to a garden together, teaching patience and responsibility. • Picnics: Pack some food and a blanket and head to the nearest park. As the Senior Patrol Leader, I was able to connect with both adults and kids who participated in the camp, which, in itself, was a reward.” As is tradition, the day camp culminated in its much-anticipated egg drop contest, where Scouts put their creative minds to the test by finding the best way to drop a raw egg from a height of seven stories without the egg breaking. Members of the Piedmont Fire Department assisted by dropping the eggs, one by one, in homemade protective enclosures from the engine’s 75-foot extension ladder. The contest is unique in that Scouts are given very little restrictions on how to achieve their goal. All that is required is the container’s dimension must measure less than 8” x 8” x 8”, the egg must be raw and campers may not affix anything to the egg itself. Other than that, “anything goes,” according to organizers. Designs this year included an egg-holding box with a parachute to slow its descent and a box of loose crash pads made from popcorn and packing peanuts. Everyone whose egg survived the fall received a free icee at Mulberry’s Market. Staffer Ciaran Gallagher helps a young camper put the finishing touches on his foam rocket. articles.text: Preview of this year’s course and favorite riders Photos courtesy of CyclingWeekly.com Tadej Pogačar looks to win his third Tour de France General Classification standings. This year’s Tour de France marks the 111th edition of La Grande Boucle, starting on Saturday, June 29 in Florence, Italy and, for the first time ever, finishes on July 21 in Nice, France, not Paris due to preparations for the Olympic Games this summer. Another intriguing item is that the Grand Finale, the last race day, will be an individual time trial, and could decide the fate of this year’s Yellow Jersey. The start in Florence marks the first time the tour will begin in Italy. The country will host the first four stages, beginning with 206 km and 200 km hilly stages to Bologna. Following a flat stage on July 3, the tour turns up for its first mountain classification on Stage 4 as they leave Italy from Pinerolo 138 km to Valloire, France. It will feature three steep climbs, including a 23 km climb up Col du Galibier before the descent to the finish. Stages 5-6 provides a collective 376 km of flat riding, which should be good days for the sprinters with both stages including individual intermediate sprints. FRIEDIE SCHICKEDANZ Flag Football & Lacrosse Friedie Schickedanz just finished her junior year at PHS and is a two-sport athlete in flag football and lacrosse. She lined up at quarterback in Piedmont’s inaugural flag football season and was an attacker in the spring on the lacrosse team. In lacrosse she was a marquee ball handler who helped PHS win its first WACC championship since 2019 in an 8-7 victory over Bishop O’Dowd. Piedmont answered a 6-5 deficit in the third quarter after allowing three consecutive goals, quickly responded with goals by Schickedanz and two Ruby Guzdar. She earned first-team All-League honors. articles.text: Kronos Quartet: Violinists David Harrington and John Sherba (left), Hank Dutt (viola) and Paul Wiancko (cello) Even after 50 years, the unique Kronos Quartet is still plunging headlong into new music with its San Francisco festival last weekend, adding uncommon extras, summed up as partly concert, partly quintet, partly historical interview, partly an exhumed Cantonese opera recording. The unorthodox concert tribute entailed a talk on Chinese-American history leading into a rousing quintet of Kronos plus Wu Man – the East meeting West squarely and amicably, pentatonic and tonality blended – in Dai Wei’s Through the Narrow Gate. Wu Man’s accomplished play plucking the strings of a Chinese pipa is extraordinary, whether blending nimbly with the four Kronos string players or doing dulcet accompaniments to an interview with former Piedmonter, historian and legal scholar David Lei – arguably the most heterogeneous interplay yet attempted at the SFJazz Center’s Miner Auditorium. Wu Man’s deft play can make cherry trees bloom. And as background for Through the Narrow Gate came, snatches of an early-20th-century Edison-cylinder recording of Cantonese opera found in an archive blended with composer Dai Wei’s own voice. Another Kronos marker was that most of the program featured women composers, including Marvel Jem Roth, Haeon Lee, Dai Wei and Aleksandra Vrebalov, with the latter winning the sought-after Gravemeyer Prize for composition this year. Here, in Gold Came from Space, Vrebalov has created a work destined to win wide acceptance, settling down after a whirlwind of tremolos to a fetching, song-like viola solo, beautifully rendered by Hank Dutt. The fearless Kronos players bite off one challenge after another, even delving into the spikiest music of recent times. These entailed on June 20 – in addition to a Sun Ra/Terry Riley adaptation – Sahba Aminikia’s Four Seasons excerpt, Zachary Watkins’ Black Body Radiance, and an arrangement of a Philip Glass piano etude – the latter the only score all night written prior to last year. Works were amplified, with several prerecorded segments, keeping sound engineer Scott Fraser on the move. The fearless Kronos players, still in lightning-fast form, included the longest tenured players David Harrington, John Sherba, Hank Dutt, and at cello newcomer Paul Wiancko. These concerts will entail a farewell to both Sherba and Dutt, two stalwarts with 35-plus years of service here. Under longtime executive director Janet Cowperthwaite, who is also stepping aside this year, Kronos is San Francisco-based. Kronos Festival, the quartet featured in the first of the June 20-23 concerts. Nightly new rep. Miner Auditorium, S.F. Jazz Center. articles.text: Asian Art Museum in San Francisco’s Phoenix Kingdoms exhibition, based on recent archaeological discoveries, is on view now through July 22. The exhibition highlights two kingdoms that flourished during China’s Bronze Age, the Zeng and Chu states, encompassing over 2,000 years of imperial history. Phoenix Kingdoms marries art and history while describing one of the most sophisticated, but forgotten, points of Chinese art and culture. The Zeng and Chu states reflect a shamanistic spirituality, rife with belief in human-animal communication, fascination with river and mountain deities, rituals filled with bell and drum music, and a proliferation of magical phoenix totems. “Drawing on the vibrant talent of its artisans and taking advantage of technological advances, the painting, sculpture, calligraphy, and music of this culturally fertile land were developed to an exceptionally high degree,” said Fan Jeremy Zhang, Asian Art Museum’s Curator of Chinese Art. “It was in Chu that a distinctive religious and philosophical tradition evolved and matured into Daoism, a rival to Confucianism that emerged largely in northern China.” “We have no record that speaks of China’s unification from the perspective of the defeated Chu people,” said Jay Xu, Museum Director and CEO. “Because they were never told by the victor, the stories of Phoenix Kingdoms have remained hidden until now.” To learn more, and to purchase tickets, visit https://exhibitions. asianart.org.

articles.text: When Kathleen Crandall saw a need in the Berkeley arts community, she took the initiative to address it. Crandall, a member of the Berkeley Symphony Board of Directors and a newly appointed member of the Berkeley Civic Arts Commission, noticed that many of the city’s arts organizations recently had appointed new leaders — but they hadn’t yet had a chance to speak to one another. “I wanted to create an opportunity for them to convene, discuss common goals, and envision collaborative opportunities,” Crandall said. “It is a challenging time for arts organizations as they rebuild their communities in the post-pandemic era. I wanted these leaders to know that they are not alone: they have each other, and they have tremendous support among business and civic leaders.” More than a dozen arts leaders attended the meeting, which took place on the campuses of Freight & Salvage and the California Jazz Conservatory in downtown Berkeley. They enjoyed a lunch catered by ACT Catering and coffee provided by the Berkeley Jazzcaffè. The event included performances by musicians from the California Jazz Conservatory, the Berkeley Symphony, and Berkeley Symphony Board member James Parrish Smith. Jen Lovvorn of the Berkeley Civic Arts Commission said, “It was just what was needed with all the new arts leaders in Berkeley – a perfect event to introduce the new directors to those who’ve been here for a while.” Clayton Shelvin, Managing Director of Freight & Salvage, agreed: “We have amazing leaders in this community and it was exciting to see what happens when we all put our minds together.” The summit concluded with a champagne reception for community leaders sponsored by The Grubb Co and Panoramic Interests and Berkeley Symphony board member Shariq Yosufzai. “The Berkeley Symphony was proud to co-host the 2024 Music & Art Summit, along with our neighbor organization Freight & Salvage,” said Marion Atherton, Berkeley Symphony Executive Director. “We really felt the outpouring of support from the community, and I am very grateful to have played a part in this event.”

articles.text: Launching tributes to the Fathers The Father of Our Country had intoned, This newborn nation needs its horses, wagons, Muskets, shock troops tough as dragons. Farmers, turned to Minute Men, now standing firm! Forgetting crops to serve their freedom term! Facing all adversity, even drown On crossing River Delaware to thwart the red-coats of the Crown! Most of all, we need Our fathers standing tall, With weapons meeting every onslaught, every call, Till victory is ours on Yorktown’s mall! And when we win, we’ll designate a day To honor them, in June or May, Which then perpetually will be the Fathers’ Day! –George Washington’s long-lost address to fighting men, unearthed just now in a musty West Coast den, inscribed with parchment, ink, and ballpoint pen. Longtime Piedmont resident Paul Hertelendy is the city’s Poet Laureate.

articles.text: With your kind permission, I’d like to look into the future of education. First, let me assert my firm belief that three subjects should be required throughout life. These three subjects are music, foreign language and sports. Put them in any order you like. Education has been a vexing problem since the beginning of education itself. The Talmud addresses the problem directly. In a loose translation, the Talmud says: “educators are self-serving bureaucrats.” When we look further into the Talmud’s comments we find that these self-serving bureaucrats are noted for having a political agenda contrary to the progress of education. It is interesting to note that the Talmud, as a text, was begun in approximately the year 200 CE. Deep thinkers have added to its content for more than 1000 years. In my opinion, education continues on a line of mediocrity. The reason for this mediocrity is simple. The bureaucrat identifies the “problem” and solves it. The real “problem” is that education bureaucrats are replaced by other bureaucrats. All of them have simplistic solutions which continue to fail, and yet they hope for a different result. Who would do such a thing? My proposal is that three subjects should be in the constant repertoire of every student. Every kid should learn to speak another language. articles.text: British film with superb performances Rachel Weisz, Rachel McAdams and Alessandro Nivola in Disobedience reach for one another. It is more than they can bear. Disobedience is both beautiful and devastating, a powerful narrative which is, from the first scene, quietly unrelenting. The film is set in the North of London and opens with Rav Krushka, a much loved leader of an orthodox Jewish community, speaking to his congregation about that ambivalent place in life that is book-ended by spirituality and goodness. The contrast is with aspects of the human heart that can be dark beyond comprehension. God, the Rav explains, has given man the power of free will, meaning the ability to choose and thereby disobey. It’s a moving and compelling sermon. And when he unexpectedly dies, his daughter, Ronit (Rachel Weisz), a photographer living in New York, is notified. She flies to London, the community where she grew up, just in time for the funeral preparations. She has been gone for some time and those still remembering her are noticeably surprised to see her. Ronit discovers that her two childhood friends, Dovid (Allesandro Nivola) and Esti (Rachel McAdams), are married. Dovid asks her to stay with them in their home. What has been part of the past for Ronit and Esti becomes part of the present and the reason for Ronit’s exile slowly is revealed. What has been an attraction long buried is slowly and intensely resurrected. Their desire for one another, their heat, is palpable; however, it is also a taboo, forbidden in this cloistered community. The dilemma they face comes raging to the fore, repressed, denied and yet overpowering. Their torment is relentlessly present, most often conveyed by a look, a glance, their eyes averted while they It is a shattering line they are helpless not to cross. And symbolizing the emotional chasm between their need for one another and the judgment of the community is Dovid, angry but decent, deeply conflicted and yet trapped by his love for Esti. Disobedience is a love story, first and foremost. But it is also about the inherent consequences, intended and unintended, that await the women. Their attraction is riven with potential ostracism from a people who have the power based upon religious belief and mores of tightly wound steel. And so Ronit and Esti are faced with that moment, spoken of at the outset by Rav Krushka, regarding free will. The only question, and the source of their anguish and hesitation, is can they summon the strength necessary to be who they are and accept that they must separate from those they have known and obeyed all of their lives. As well as, of course, Esti’s husband, Dovid. This is a wonderfully told film, powerful in its muted conversations in grey tones and the coldness of deep winter. It is also a narrative about all that is forbidden, yet impossible to deny, which ultimately is about one’s identity. The sense of crushing repression and fervency are made starkly clear by the stunning performances of Weisz and McAdams, to include a superb supporting cast in a film that is gripping, ruinous and deeply human. Disobedience. Directed by Sebastian Lelio. Starring Rachel Weisz, Rachel McAdams, Allesandra Nivera. 1 hr., 54 min. Rated R. Released in 2017. Streaming on VUDUF/Netflix/Prime/ Apple tv

articles.text: A scene from Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit Kids will love Wallace & Gromit, an Oscar-winning franchise of 30-minute shorts, plus one feature. The first short was A Grand Day, followed by The Wrong Trousers, A Close Shave, and A Matter of Loaf and Death. The Curse of the Were-Rabbit was the Aardman studio’s first Claymation feature film. The stars of the franchise are, of course, Wallace (Peter Sallis), a suburban Brit with a pearshaped head and wide, ear-to-ear smile, and his faithful, industrious, ever-silent Beagle (graduate of the Dogwart Academy). They live together in a house filled with labor saving inventions and Rube Goldberg-like contraptions, invented by Wallace, whose day jobs include window cleaner and baker. In Were-Rabbit, he is the owner of the Anti-Pesto Services, a pest control company. His current responsibility is to keep the village gardens free of vegetable-eating rabbits. He, of course, has an invention just for this purpose, a vacuum that sucks up the rabbits, which he keeps in his basement. All of this is in preparation for the Town’s annual vegetable growing competition, the winning prize being a golden carrot. One evening, using his invention, Wallace captures a rabbit who is eating Lady Tottington’s (Helena Bonham Carter) veggies. Unfortunately, his contraption has a miscalculation, and he creates a gigantic Were-Rabbit that is ravenous for vegetables, and is chomping its way through garden after village garden, something that will surely upset the coming veggie-growing contest. Hearing of this garden emergency, Lord Victor Quartermaine (Ralph Fiennes) volunteers to hunt down the culprit with his rifle and shoot it; however lady Tottington objects, and convinces the town folk to allow Wallace and his Anti-Pesto Services to take care of the problem. The mystery that Wallace must solve is, who or what is this Were-Rabbit? It’s a puzzle that takes Wallace and Gromit on an adventure. Wallace even discovers giant muddy footprints that lead into his house. What is going on, Wallace wonders? And even Gromit, who is highly intelligent, can’t figure out the source of the footprints. There are lots of surprises and chases, even threats by Quartermaine to kill the Were-Rabbit with a golden bullet. Things get more than a bit chaotic, involving at one point an airborne dogfight between Gromit and Q.’s dog Phillip. There’s a bit of light romance thrown in (Wallace and Lady T. have some chemistry). Mostly, it’s all daffy fun, wonderfully creative and involves lots of pratfalls and puns. Youngsters will be smitten. And adults will howl over the puns. Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit. Claymation by Aardman Animations. Directed by Nick Park. With voices of Peter Sallis, Ralph Fiennes, Helena Bonham-Carter. 1 hr., 25 min. Rated G. Released 2015. Streaming on Peacock/Fandango/prime/apple tv. By Jay Russell For the City of Piedmont’s centennial anniversary in January 2007, the City installed 10 historic land markers to create the Piedmont Park History Trail. These markers shine a light on the wonders that were in the park not so long ago. The map of the history trail outlining all the markers can be found in front of the Veterans’ Hall on the corner of Highland and Vista Avenue. The first marker is on the patio in front of City Hall. Stop by and stoke up on your Piedmont history on your next essential dog walk. Marker 1: Faux Bois Benches Frank C. Havens developed Piedmont Park between 1898 and 1920. Using eucalyptus saplings and branch stickwork, he had 3,000 rustic wood benches constructed and placed throughout the park. An article in the Oakland Tribune dated May 5, 1898 described the park at the time. “[Seating accommodations] have been admirably supplied by the scattering in every direction The original benches were made out of eucalyptus and installed throughout Piedmont Park at the turn of the 20th century. Marker #1 of the Piedmont Park History Trail is on the patio in front of City Hall and describes the origin of the faux bois benches. of 3,000 settees made of eucalyptus. They throng the walks near the music stand, grace the side of the streamlet, cluster about trees and in some places muster in such forces as to be intended for the use of picnic parties,” the article stated. But the wooded benches proved to be prone to falling apart. Because of the homespun frontier look, people liked them so much in the 1920’s the city made some faux bois (fake wood) replica park benches out of concrete. The park had faux bois benches through the early part of the 20th Century. The only remaining bench was kept at the Corporation Yard, and in 2001 in attempting to restore it, the bench collapsed. During the city’s 100th anniversary in January 2007, a new concrete bench was created and lowered into place on the patio in front of City Hall. Given its weight and girth, it is the one public bench that doesn’t need to be bolted to the ground. The decision to build the original benches with eucalyptus is a clue to a larger story about the development of California. Frank C. Havens owned a eucalyptus nursery in the Lakeshore area. In his lifetime the hills surrounding Piedmont were largely bare due to the clear-cutting of pine, cedar and redwood to rebuild houses in San Francisco destroyed by the fire following the 1906 earthquake. Havens imported and planted millions of eucalyptus saplings on a 14-mile strip of the hills for a hardwood forest, knowing that eucalyptus was a fast-growing tree. At the time he was unaware that it was used in other locations primarily as pulp for paper or firewood, but not building materials. As a pioneer in introducing eucalyptus to the region, Havens is partially responsible for today’s vast prevalence of non-native Eucalyptus trees in the Oakland and Berkeley hills. Eucalyptus tends to take over areas, sending roots horizontally and growing quickly. Eucalyptus rapidly drinks up water and nutrients in the soil. Native trees can’t compete, and grass can’t grow under the dense canopy and oily leaf cover. Eucalyptus trees are not without fans however for their beauty, useful oil and as koala food. The faux bois benches serve as a gateway seat to our past. There are history lessons all around us. The focus of Jim Kellogg’s tour was the distinctive architectural character of early Piedmont, beginning in 1907 when Piedmont was incorporated. The city’s character was influenced by many families from around the country who moved to Piedmont in early 1900 and wanted their new homes to recall the architectural style from their childhood. On last week’s walk, the city center provided the opportunity to see examples of more than a half dozen architectural styles: French Colonial, Victorian, English Tutor, Colonial Revival, American Foursquare, Bungalow and Craftsman. The walk was a little less than two miles and focused on the historic central area of the city, including Vista, Hillside and Bonita Avenues. The walkers stopped at 225 Hillside to talk about the beautiful Queen Anne Shingle Style house and then gathered for a group photo. As they were getting ready to move on, the homeowner, Alissa Welch, came out and graciously told the group about her family’s work on the house. Further down Hillside, the walkers noted one of the last remaining original street lamps in Piedmont and studied homes designed by well-known Bay Area architects at that time, including: Albert Farr, Charles Dickey, and the firm Bakewell and Brown. Interesting stories about the people who shaped the character of early Piedmont were shared with the walkers. The famous architect Albert Farr’s favorite carpenter was known as “One-Nail” MacGregor because as a Scotsman he was known to have said “Build homes quickly and efficiently, and don’t use two nails when one nail will do.” All of the homes were beautiful and appreciated by the walkers. So was Jim’s preparation and the knowledge he shared with the group. He will come back soon for another tour with the group. People who want to learn more about the early history and architecture of Piedmont were encouraged to purchase a copy of “Cottages and Castles: The Centennial Houses of the City of Piedmont”, by Ann Swift. This was published in 2007 and a limited number of copies are still available at Piedmont City Hall for $30. articles.text: How do I figure out the proper fix? Dear Jim: I have noticed over the last few years that my foundation and drainage problems are getting worse. I have cracks in my living room, water in my crawlspace, and my foundation doesn’t look great. I have talked to a bunch of Contractors and they all tell me something different. Why this disparity in solutions? And how do I figure out what my house really needs? Unfortunately, this is the same story I hear every day. “What Long term drainage issues ruined this foundation. Plastic covering the soil and plywood for seismic did not help with the real problem. Improper repairs can often lead to structural issues. These patched together supports under the front landing eventually made things worse. should I do?” The good news is that there is likely one best answer to your structural woes. You just have to talk to the right person. The “Why” Behind the Confusion In simplest terms, most General Contractors lack the background and insight to provide you with the best solution. These problems are often wholistic, involving multiple structural components that are all interacting- drainage, foundation, framing and structure, seismic, etc. It takes a lot of experience, specifically with residential structural work and drainage, to be able to find the best solution in the short window of an initial meeting. And the problem may be very different from what you suspect- most commonly that your foundation issues and cracks are mostly related to faulty drainage that also needs to be addressed. Timing is also a big issue. Structural problems are sometimes fast developing, but most often have been brewing for decades. Everyone wants to know “when” these repairs need to be made, and whether or not they are serious issues. The Reality You Need to Consider Fou ndation and d rainage issues cannot typically be “fixed”. Older foundations in poor condition generally need to be replaced. Most drainage issues occur because you have no real drainage system when you need one. Short term repairs can make your problems worse. Proper solutions can be expensive work that most aren’t looking forward to. And often drainage, foundation, and seismic repairs are best done all together. The bottom line is that you need to do what is best long term for your home and avoid short-term fixes unless you have an immediate problem. It shouldn’t need to be a question of what- just a question of when. Conversations with Your Local Contractor is a feature by Jim and Lisa Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. articles.text: If you’ve retired, you may have thought you closed the book on one chapter of your life. But what happens if you need to “reverse” your retirement? Due to higher inflation and rising interest rates, many retirees are taking out more money from their retirement accounts than they had originally anticipated. As a result, some are headed back to the workforce. If you’re thinking of joining them, you’ll need to consider some factors that may affect your finances. First, if you’ve been taking Social Security, be aware that you could lose some of your benefits if you earn over a certain level, at least until you reach your full retirement age, which is likely between 66 and 67. Specifically, if you are under your full retirement age for the entire year, Social Security will deduct $1 from your benefit payments for every $2 you earn above the annual limit, which, in 2024, is $22,320. In the year you reach your full retirement age, Social Security will deduct $1 in benefits for every $3 you earn above a different limit, which, in 2024, is $59,520. Social Security will only count your earnings up to the month before you reach your full retirement age, at which point your earnings will no longer reduce your benefits, regardless of how much you earn. Also, Social Security will recalculate your benefit amounts to credit you for the months your payments were reduced due to your excess earnings. Social Security also allows you to pay back early benefits received if you withdraw your application within 12 months of starting benefits. This move could help you receive substantially higher benefits at full retirement age. Your Social Security isn’t the only benefit that could be affected by your earnings. Your Medicare Part B and Part D premiums are based on your income, so they could rise if you start earning more money. Also, your extra income could push you into a higher tax bracket. Nonetheless, you can certainly gain some benefits by returning to the working world. Obviously, you’ll be making money that can help you boost your daily cash flow and possibly reduce some debts. But depending on where you work, you might also be able to contribute to a 401(k) or other employer-sponsored retirement plan. And regardless of where you work, you’ll be eligible to contribute to an IRA. By putting more money into these accounts, you may well be able to strengthen your financial position during your retirement years. You might also be able to receive some employee benefits, such as group health insurance – which could be particularly valuable if you haven’t yet started receiving Medicare. In addition to the potential financial advantages of going back to work, you might get some social benefits, too. Many people enjoy the interactions with fellow workers and miss these exchanges when they retire, so a return to the workforce, even if it’s on a part-time basis, may give you an emotional boost. In the final analysis, you’ll want to weigh the potential costs of going back to work against the possible benefits. There’s no one right answer for everyone, but by looking at all the variables, you should be able to reach a decision that works for you. Tadej Pogačar – UAE Team Emirates Can Slovenia’s Tadej Pogačar win his third Tour de France after winning in 2020 and 2021? Despite finishing as the runner up for the last two years, the 25-yearold is still this year’s favorite. The amount of mountain climbs certainly plays well towards his odds after winning polka-dot jersey as the tour’s best mountain rider in 2020 and 2021. Jonas Vingegaard – Visma–Lease a Bike Despite winning the Yellow Jersey in 2022 and 2023, Danish rider Jonas Vingegaard is considered the No. 2 candidate to win this year’s General Classification. At 27-years-old, he should also benefit from the large number of mountain classifications. He’s trying to become the first three-peat winner since Chris Froome accomplished the feat from 2015-2017. Primož Roglič – Bora–Hansgrohe Fellow Slovenian Primož Roglič, 34, was leading the 2020 Tour de France entering the second-to-last stage before his countryman Pogačar took the lead in a breathtaking Stage 20 time trial last year. Roglič left Vingegaard’s team in October 2023 for Bora-Hansgrohe. Remco Evenepoel – Soudal–Quick-Step 24-year-old Belgian, Remco Evenepoel, is odds makers’ fourth favorite. He recently finished seventh in the Critérium du Dauphiné earlier this month from June 2-9. He won the Volta ao Algarve and Figueira Champions Classic in February. Matteo Jorgenson – Visma–Lease a Bike Matteo Jorgenson winning the tour seems less likely because he’s teammates with Vingegaard, meaning he’ll likely be a role player in helping push the Dane forward. But the 24-yearold makes the list because he’s a local boy from Walnut Creek. He placed 20th in 2022 but did not finish in 2023.
